lesson.menu_desc: A checkpoint for Lessons 17-23 on a real stage: the Jewelers' Forum in New York holds a formal debate on the question every jeweler is asking (should a luxury brand sell lab-grown diamonds?), and Milton speaks against Claire, a retail buyer. Put all the advanced structures to work in one argument (third and mixed conditionals, provided that and unless, what-clefts, used to, gerunds and infinitives, what if) and learn the language of debate: stance, rebuttal, counterargument, concede, compelling, drawback, outweigh, consensus — 35 slides

defs: To admit that the other person is right about something
A disadvantage or a problem that makes something less attractive
An answer that tries to show that the other side's argument is wrong
An agreement that all or most people in a group accept
A public opinion or position on an issue

items.situation: The moderator asks for your position on lab-grown diamonds. Say it in one sentence.
Claire makes a good point about price. Admit it, but keep your position.
Say when you would accept lab-grown stones in your store.
Tell the audience how your industry was twenty years ago.
Connect a past decision of the industry with today's problem.
Ask the audience a hypothetical question to make them think.

listenings.text: Good evening, and welcome to the Jewelers' Forum here in New York. I'm Diane Foster, and I'll be your moderator tonight. Our motion is simple, but it divides our whole industry: a luxury jeweler should sell lab-grown diamonds. Let me explain the format. Each speaker has two minutes for an opening statement, one minute for a rebuttal, and one minute to close. Please keep to the time, unless I ask you to continue. Before we start, the audience votes. Right now, fifty-five percent of you are against the motion. If we had held this debate ten years ago, I think almost nobody would vote for it. What we want tonight is not a winner. It's a clear argument from both sides. At the end, you vote again, and we'll see whether anybody changed their stance. Our first speaker is Claire Bennett, a buyer for a chain of department stores. She will speak for the motion. Against the motion, we have Milton Sayegh, an exporter of fine jewelry from Brazil. Claire, the floor is yours.

My name is Henry Walsh, and I've been a gemologist for thirty years. People often ask me which diamond is better. My answer always surprises them. Under the microscope, a lab-grown diamond is a real diamond. It has the same chemistry, the same hardness and the same fire. So the question isn't about the stone. It's about the story. Twenty years ago, customers used to ask only two questions: how big is it, and how much is it? Today they want to know where the stone came from. That's a compelling reason to think carefully about what we sell. I concede that lab-grown stones have one big advantage, which is the price. But there's a drawback that many buyers forget. They lose value very fast, because factories can make more every year. If I were buying a ring for my wife, I would want something rare. My advice to jewelers is simple. Sell both if you want, provided that you tell the customer the truth. What destroys a luxury brand is not the product. It's a customer who feels lied to.
